activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft, and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud.
story:
Emmett had four days to learn the whole last page of "March of the Snow Kings," and the trumpet part looked like someone had spilled alphabet soup on it. Letters and squiggles crowded the staff: p, f, more p's, more f's. He sat in the music room after school with his trumpet on his lap, glaring at the sheet music while the radiator clanked and the smell of floor wax rose from the tiles.

"Mr. Wu says we run it Friday," said Abbygail, dropping her flute case on the next chair. "Full run-through, no stopping. If we sound terrible, he moves the concert back a week and everybody's parents find out why."

"The trumpets always sound terrible at the end," Emmett said. "We blast the last eight bars like a fire alarm." It was true. Every rehearsal, the whole section cruised along fine until the final line, and then the room got so loud that Mr. Wu would press his hands flat in the air and say "gentler, gentle giants" in that tired voice of his.

Ernest wandered in carrying his drumsticks. He leaned over Emmett's music and tapped the last line. "There's your problem. See those letters? Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft. And fortissimo, written ff, means very loud." He pointed at the bar before the ending, which was stamped with a fat ff, then at the final bars, marked pp. "You're playing the loud part and the soft part at the same volume. Loud."

Emmett squinted at the page. The ff was in the middle of the big climax, and the pp came after, right at the quiet ending. That meant the kings in the piece weren't charging offstage in glory. They were tiptoeing away. The whole ending was supposed to shrink, and the trumpets were flattening it. "So we've been ending a monarchy-style coronation parade when the music actually wants the whole court sneaking off to bed," he said.

"Sure," said Ernest. "Whatever that means, yes."

Emmett tried a test. He played the ff bar big, letting it fill the room until the sound bounced off the piano in the corner, then dropped his breath way down for the pp bars so the notes came out thin as a whisper of wind under a door. Abbygail put down her flute and listened. "Do that again," she said, so he did. The second time the change felt smoother, like stepping off a ladder onto a carpet.

They ran the ending together, flute and trumpet, five times through. On the sixth try Emmett relaxed too much and the soft part vanished completely, no sound at all, just air. Ernest laughed and called it "the invisible trumpet," which Emmett had to admit was fair. Controversial as it was among the trumpets, who all believed a march should end huge, Emmett decided he would defend the quiet ending to anybody. He circled the pp in pencil and wrote TINY above it.

Friday came, and Mr. Wu counted them in with his baton. The band rumbled through the Snow Kings, gathered speed toward the climax, and hit the ff bar so hard that a music stand buzzed. Then Emmett caught Abbygail's eye across the room, pulled his breath down, and let the last eight bars fall away to almost nothing. The other trumpets followed him. The music shrank and shrank until it was barely a thread of sound, and then it stopped, and the radiator clanked once into the silence.

Mr. Wu lowered his baton slowly. "Well," he said. "That's the first time I've actually heard the ending. Somebody get the trumpets some water, they've earned it."

Abbygail grinned across the stands and held up her flute like a trophy. Emmett wiped his mouthpiece on his sleeve and flipped his music back to page one, ready to go again.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
story:
Jessica stood in her grandmother's kitchen with a plate of pineapple and mango, listening to her cousins argue about whether fruit counted as a carbohydrate, when Tina nudged her elbow. "Did you bring your practice book?"

"Of course." Jessica had been carrying the blue book everywhere for three weeks. Her bat mitzvah was in one month, and she had to chant her Torah portion by heart, every word, every melody. The book had vowels under the letters and little musical marks above them, like tiny stairs telling her voice where to go. She could do the first eight verses without stumbling now.

The family gathering moved out to the patio, where Uncle somebody had strung lights and set up a table of tropical fruit salad next to the potato salad nobody touched. Mr. Sandhu, the neighbour who had been invited because he always fixed Grandpa's fence, asked what the blue book was for. Jessica showed him. "I'm chanting this at my ceremony," she said, and demonstrated a verse, her finger tracking the notes.

"Where's the actual scroll you'll read from?" Tina asked.

"At the synagogue," Jessica said. Then she paused. She had never actually seen it. Her whole practice had happened in this book. She tried to picture the scroll and realized she was picturing the page in front of her, vowels and all, and something about that bothered her. What if the scroll looked different?

She had a way to test it. Her cousin had been married last spring, and the wedding video was on Grandpa's tablet. Jessica found the moment when the groom read from the scroll. She paused the video and leaned close. The letters on the parchment were bare. No vowels. No little stairs. Nothing.

"That's the problem," she said slowly. "I've been learning the tune from the printed book. The scroll doesn't have any of the marks."

"So how does anybody sing it?" Tina said.

"You just have to know it already," Jessica said. "You learn the melody in advance from the book, and then the scroll is only letters." She looked at the video frame, then at her own book, and thought about all those mornings she had hummed the melody while reading the printed page. She could have been testing herself the whole time by covering the vowels. A month was still enough time, probably. She thought about asking the rabbi on Sunday, then decided she would just start tonight.

Her grandmother's phone buzzed on the table. It was a message from Jessica's mother, who had left early to help set up for the synagogue's open house: "Rabbi says you can see the real scroll at rehearsal Tuesday. Bring your book." Jessica held the phone up so Tina could see.

"Tuesday," Tina said. "You'll cover the vowels before then, right?"

"Tonight," Jessica said, and reached for her blue book.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 3 of the Canadian Charter gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and provincial legislatures.
story:
Charles had the constitution booklet open on his knees, but the words kept sliding off his brain like water off a waxed car. Ms. Ivanova had said the class would each explain one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms at city hall on Friday, in their own words, and Charles still didn't have his. Brycen had picked freedom of expression, which was easy because Brycen never stopped talking anyway. Charlee had picked the right to be safe from unreasonable search, which sounded exciting, like a detective show.

Charles flipped to Section 3 and read it again. Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly. He squinted at it. It mentioned the House of Commons and something called a legislative assembly. Did that mean the provinces? He wondered how anyone could check a thing like that, a rule hiding inside a rule.

"Come on," his mother said from the kitchen. "We're walking past city hall anyway. There's a polling station set up there for the byelection."

At city hall, a line of adults curled along the wall beneath the big stone staircase. Charles spotted a laminated sign near the doors and stopped. It listed who could vote: Canadian citizens, and residents of the province, voting for a member of the House of Commons or the provincial legislature. He read it twice. So the legislative assembly was the provincial legislature, the same thing with two names. The sign was like a mirror of Section 3, only plainer.

He tried an experiment, the way he tested ideas in science class. He walked up to the clerk at the table, an older man with reading glasses on a chain, and asked, "Could I vote? I live here and I go to school here."

The clerk shook his head, smiling. "You have to be a citizen and of voting age, and this is for electing a member for the House of Commons or the provincial legislature. Adults only, I'm afraid."

"It says that in Section 3," Charles said. "I was hoping it would work for me anyway."

"Nice try," the clerk said. "Come back in a few years and rebel at the ballot box instead of at me."

Charlee was in the lobby with her aunt, waiting to vote, and Charles told her his discovery in a rush. On Friday, standing in front of the class in the same marble hall, he held up the booklet and said, "Section 3 says every Canadian citizen has the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and the provincial legislatures. I couldn't picture the legislative part, so I checked the sign at the polling station downstairs, and it matched." He pointed at the doors, where the line was still moving, voter by voter, through the turbulent crowd of noon-hour pedestrians outside. "It's happening right now, one floor below us."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
The rumor reached Anais before lunch: the school board was going to tear down the old oak by the cafeteria to build a bike rack. "It's true," Haroun insisted, dropping his tray beside hers. "My cousin heard the principal say it." Anais looked out the window at the tree, its broad canopy shading half the courtyard, where kids ate on hot days and where Margo had once found a robin's egg in the grass. Losing it seemed both bizarre and possible, because the school did strange things sometimes.

She wanted the truth, not just a feeling. That night she asked her dad, who was watching a political ad on TV and grumbling at it. He waved his phone at the screen. "See this claim? I look these up on PolitiFact. It's a fact-checking website, started in 2007. They rate things on a scale they call the Truth-O-Meter." He turned the phone so she could see the little gauge graphic. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire." Anais leaned closer. A rumor, she realized, was like the ad: somebody said it, but nobody had checked it.

The next morning she found Margo at the courtyard picnic table under the oak. "We need to test the rumor," Anais said. "Like a fact-checker." Margo raised an eyebrow. "How? It's not on any website." Anais spread her notebook. "We find the evidence. First, the principal's office. If the school board really voted on it, there'd be a record." They walked to the front office together, and Anais asked the secretary if she could see the minutes from the last board meeting. The secretary printed one page.

There it was, agenda item seven: bicycle parking expansion, proposed for the gravel lot behind the gym. Nothing about the oak. Anais read it twice, feeling her shoulders drop with relief. But Haroun still looked doubtful when they found him at recess. "My cousin heard it," he repeated. "Haroun," Anais said, "your cousin's opinion isn't a fact. Anyone can believe something. A claim you can check, that's different." She held up the printed page. "I checked. The tree stays."

Haroun squinted at the paper, then at the oak, then broke into a grin. "Okay. Pants on Fire for my cousin." They sat together under the canopy while Margo pulled out her sandwich, and Anais wrote one line in her notebook: "Checked, True." Somewhere above them a robin sang, and she thought tomorrow she'd look up one more thing on that website, just to see what the little gauge would say.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.
story:
Easton stood in front of a glass case at the history museum, staring at a small leather book with cracked edges. "It's a settler's diary," Izabella said, reading the label beside him. "From 1873." Deklan leaned over Easton's shoulder, close enough that Easton could hear him breathing. "A diary? We're supposed to use this to explain why people moved west? It doesn't exactly say anything on the cover."

"It doesn't have to," Easton said. Ms. Chea had handed each of them a worksheet with one question on it: use a primary source to explain westward movement. The diary was the only primary source in the room that wasn't a locked map or a rusty plow. Easton bent close to the glass and copied the faded handwriting into his notebook, line by line. "March the fourth. We have staked our claim at last. One hundred sixty acres, and it is ours if we stay." He read it twice, then wrote it down. "Ours if we stay."

Something tugged at his memory. Last summer, at his grandpa's house, he had found a stiff paper folded inside an old Bible, brown at the creases. He had carried it to the kitchen, and his grandpa had smoothed it flat on the table with both palms, careful as a man handling a bird. "This is how our family got the farm," his grandpa had said. "It's a Homestead Act paper. The United States gave 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years." Easton had asked why anyone would give away land, and his grandpa had laughed. "They weren't giving it away, exactly. You paid with five years of your life." Then he'd let Easton hold it, saying, "Careful, now. That's the whole reason we're here."

Back at the museum, Easton tapped his pencil against the notebook. The diary said "ours if we stay." His grandpa's paper had said the same thing in official language. He flipped to the next page of the diary, and here was the test: if land was the reason, the settler should write about land again, and not just about adventure or gold. "April the tenth. We have turned four acres of sod. The wheat will need the bees to pollinate it if we plant an orchard too, so William is keeping two hives." Easton grinned. Four acres out of one hundred sixty. This man was farming, staying, counting acres. It wasn't a story about wandering. It was a claim.

"Listen," Easton said, and read both quotes aloud to Izabella and Deklan. "That's why they moved west. Free land, if they farmed it for five years." Deklan frowned. "But the diary never says that exactly." "It doesn't have to be explicit," Izabella said, pointing at the sod line. "He shows it. That's better than saying it." Ms. Chea wandered over, glanced at Easton's notebook, and raised her eyebrows at the two copied entries side by side. "You found a pattern," she said. "Where's your evidence from your own life?" Easton slid his worksheet across and told them about the paper in the Bible. "An anecdote isn't evidence," Deklan whispered, and Izabella elbowed him. "It is when you have the actual paper."

On the way out, Easton stopped at the case one more time and pressed his palm flat against the cool glass, right beside the little book.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
story:
The driving school shared a parking lot with a laundromat, which was why Kayla's mother had signed her up for the Saturday "home skills" class in the back room of Tehrani's Driving Academy while she took her own lesson out on the road. Ms. Tehrani, who owned the place, taught parallel parking in the front and let the class use the little side room with its washer, dryer, and long folding table. Today Kayla wanted to finish a whole load alone, from sorting colors to folding, because last time she had needed help with every step and Marko had teased her about it for a week.

She sorted first: darks in one pile, whites in another, the red t-shirt by itself because it had turned Marko's socks pink the last time. She measured the soap, started the washer, and while it ran she noticed something odd about the dryer. Marko ran a test load the week before and his towels had taken two full cycles to dry. Hers would be finished in one. She stood in front of the machine with her arms crossed, thinking. Same dryer, same heat setting. Two cycles versus one. That was an anomaly, and anomalies usually meant something was going on that you couldn't see.

She pulled out the lint filter. It was matted thick with grey fuzz, packed down like felt, so heavy she could almost peel it off in one piece. Nobody in the class had been cleaning it, probably because nobody had been assigned the job. She held it up to the light by the window. "Ms. Tehrani," she called, "is it true that failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires?" Ms. Tehrani poked her head in from the front room, still holding her clipboard of brake-test scores. "That's what the U.S. Fire Administration says," she answered. "They track that sort of thing." Then she went back to her student, who was digesting the rules of the road one confusing intersection at a time.

Kayla peeled the lint off the screen and dropped it in the trash, then ran the filter under the tap the way her mother did at home. She slid it back in and, when her wash finished, loaded the wet clothes and set the timer for one cycle. If her idea about the hidden blockage was right, they would dry in one. While the drum tumbled, she thought about Marko's two-cycle towels, and about how she had laughed along with his teasing instead of asking why his load had taken so long. Maybe next time she would ask why first and laugh later. Or maybe not. She hadn't decided.

The buzzer sounded. She opened the door and pulled out a warm, completely dry towel, folded it into thirds, and stacked it on the table, corners matched, edges even. When Marko walked in for the afternoon session, she was lining up the last of the shirts. "Fifteen minutes," she said, pointing at the dryer. "What's your record?"

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In American English, a comma or period that ends a quotation goes inside the closing quotation marks; British usage often places it outside.
story:
Carter slouched into Room 12 with four minutes before the writing club bell, holding his story like it might bite him. The anonymous contest entries were due at the end of the meeting, and his story about a beekeeper who had once been a refugee, searching a strange new town for a single flowering plant that bees could pollinate, still had red slashes all over the dialogue.

"They came from Maya," he said, dropping into the chair beside Lea-Rose. "My pen pal. In Manchester. I sent her my draft and she marked every single line of my dialogue wrong." He spread the pages on the desk, where they smelled faintly of her envelope, like rain and somebody's kettle. Every quotation mark in his story had a red circle around it.

Nikolai leaned over and squinted. "You put the comma inside the quotes. Like, 'I'm going to the hive,' she said. She wants it outside."

"She didn't just want it outside," Carter said. "She wrote WRONG in capital letters, three times, and once she drew a tiny angry face." He tapped the page. "But Mr. Chukwu taught us the comma goes inside. In September. I remember because I got it right on the quiz and Nikolai didn't."

"I got seven out of ten," Nikolai said with dignity. "One of them was a trick."

The bell rang, and Mr. Chukwu called from the front, "Thirty minutes until entries go in the envelope, everyone. The envelope does not negotiate." Lea-Rose was already scribbling her final draft, pencil scratching like a mouse in a wall, and the room hummed with it. Carter stared at his red circles and felt his stomach sink. If he fixed them, he might be wrong here. If he left them, Maya thought he was wrong there.

Then he sat up so fast his chair squeaked. He grabbed Maya's letter and flipped it over, searching her handwriting, her own little postscript story about her little brother and a jar of marmalade. There. Her own dialogue, in her own ink: a period sitting outside the closing quotation marks, plain as a puddle. She wasn't correcting him to be mean. She was correcting him to be British.

He turned to Lea-Rose, waving the letter. "Look. She writes it that way herself. In England the comma or the period goes outside the quotation marks. In America we put them inside. We're both right, we're just from different countries." He grinned so wide it hurt a little. "Maya's been grading me against a whole different rulebook."

"That's the twist," Lea-Rose said. "Your story has a twist about punctuation. That's deeply strange and I respect it."

Carter copied his final draft fast, comma tucked inside every quotation mark the American way, and at the bottom of his entry he added a line to the contest judges: dialogue punctuated to United States standard. Then he dug out paper for a letter. "Dear Maya," he wrote, tongue between his teeth. "Your angry faces were scientifically unjustified. Enclosed: proof. Also, how's the marmalade situation?"

At the front of the room, Mr. Chukwu licked the envelope and held it open. "Last call," he said.

Carter slid his story in and kept writing his letter, all the way past the bell.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from the Rhineland, the region of western Germany along the Rhine River next to France, so it could act as a buffer zone.
story:
Christopher had exactly one hour before the doors of the city archive closed, and one giant question to answer for Ms. Foster's class: how did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War? He raced up the stone steps two at a time, his notebook flapping, and skidded to a stop at the front desk.

"I need maps," he said. "Old ones. Germany, France, after the First World War."

The archivist raised an eyebrow, then led him past shelves of boxed photographs to a long table under a green lamp. Kiana and Hugh were already there, waving him over. They had spread out three maps, and Hugh had his finger on one of them, tapping a stretch of land along a winding river.

"Okay, so here's Germany," Hugh said. "And here's France. But look at this part. It's German land, right? It's inside Germany's borders. So why does our book say German troops weren't allowed to be there?"

Christopher leaned over the map so far his nose nearly touched the paper. The river curled through the western edge of Germany, right up against France. "The Rhine," he read off the label. "And this whole region next to it, that's the Rhineland."

"That's what it says here," Kiana said, holding up a photocopy of the treaty. "The Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from the Rhineland."

"But it's Germany's own territory," Christopher said. His brain felt like it was spinning its wheels. Why would a country be banned from putting its own soldiers on its own land? He traced the border with his finger, west from the Rhineland, and hit France immediately. Then he sat back so fast he nearly knocked over the lamp.

"Wait," he said. "It's right next to France. No German soldiers right next to France. That means France has this... empty space between it and the German army."

Hugh grabbed a pencil and drew a rectangle around the Rhineland. "Like a wall."

"Not a wall," Christopher said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "More like a cushion. A buffer zone. If Germany ever wanted to attack France, its troops couldn't even line up at the border first. France could breathe."

Kiana wrote buffer zone in her notebook and underlined it twice. "So that's the treaty protecting France," she said. "But how does that help cause another war?"

Christopher stared at the map. He thought about how angry he'd felt when his older brother got to stay up late and he didn't, how unfair it had seemed, how he'd stayed obstinate about it for a whole week. Now imagine a whole country feeling that way, he thought. A piece of your own land where your own soldiers weren't allowed.

"Think of it like this," he said. "A punishment that's too harsh doesn't make the loser behave. It makes them furious. And furious people look for a way out." He flipped to the map from ten years later, the one Hugh had found in another drawer. The dates swam past him. Germany had changed, like an animal whose adaptation to a bad situation was to grow sharper teeth, and later the troops came back into the Rhineland, and after that everything migrated from bad to worse, sliding downhill like water finding a crack in the rock.

"That's it," Christopher said, grabbing his pen. "That's my whole essay. Kiana, hold the map still. Hugh, read me that treaty line one more time, word for word."

Hugh held the photocopy up to the green light and read, "The Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from the Rhineland, the region of western Germany along the Rhine River next to France, so it could act as a buffer zone."

Christopher wrote it down, then circled France, the Rhine, and the Rhineland in one big loop of blue ink. "Ms. Foster is going to flip," he said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: StoryCorps is a project in which people record interviews with family members, and with permission the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress.
story:
Paisley had exactly three days left before Grandpa Joe flew home, and she still hadn't gotten him to talk about his childhood for the family history project. Every time she asked, he waved his hand and changed the subject to agriculture, which was his favorite topic because he had grown up on a farm. "Nobody wants to hear an old man ramble," he said on Tuesday night, stacking his plate in the sink.

So Paisley did what she did when a problem wouldn't budge: she made a plan on notebook paper. She had noticed something. Grandpa never talked about himself when she asked questions, but yesterday at the park he had told a whole story about a runaway goat, and he hadn't even been asked. The pattern was hiding in plain sight. Direct questions made him clam up, but side-by-side activities, walking, shelling peas, watching ducks, loosened him like a jar lid under hot water. She was a little skeptical of her own theory, since one goat story wasn't exactly proof, but she decided to test it.

On Friday afternoon she marched him to Willow Park with two foil-wrapped sandwiches and her phone in her back pocket. They sat on the bench by the duck pond, and sure enough, when she handed him a sandwich and said nothing about history, he started talking. He told her about walking two miles to a one-room school, about his brother's paper route, about the summer the creek flooded and the whole town turned out with sandbags.

"Phoenix told me about this thing," Paisley said between bites, pulling out her phone. "It's called StoryCorps. People record interviews with family members, and with permission the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress." She held the phone flat between them. "Like, forever. In Washington."

Grandpa went quiet, and she thought she had ruined it. Then he said, "The Library of Congress. That's where they keep Lincoln's stuff." He looked at the ducks for a long moment. "You think they'd want a farm kid's stories in a place like that?"

"They keep everybody's," Paisley said. "That's the whole point."

He straightened his cap. "Well then. Ask your questions, girl. We've got until dark."

She pressed record.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note's pitch depends on how fast the sound source vibrates: faster vibration makes a higher pitch, and slower vibration makes a lower one.
story:
Rachel stood in the wings of the school auditorium, holding her rented violin, and tried not to look at the empty seats that would be full in three days. The spring concert felt imminent, and her solo in the middle of the orchestra piece still sounded wrong. Every time she reached the long open A string note, something was off, though she could not say what.

"You're flat," said Karina, who played second violin and had come over during the break. "Not a lot. Just enough to sound sad."

"But my fingers aren't even down on that note," Rachel said. "It's an open string. How can it be flat if I'm not touching it?" Karina shrugged and went back to her chair, but Rachel turned the problem over in her mind. A pressed note could be flat if your finger slipped. An open string had no finger to blame.

She found a quiet corner behind the velvet curtain and plucked the A string, listening hard. Then, without deciding to, she nudged the tuning peg a tiny bit and plucked again. The note sank lower. She loosened the peg a little more and the note dropped further, wobbling like a dying balloon. She tightened it back and the pitch climbed. Rachel sat very still on an amp case, holding the violin in the dusty light. The string was vibrating, she could see the blur of it, and the pitch moved when she changed the vibration. Faster must mean higher, slower must mean lower. Her string had been vibrating too slowly all week, drifting flat so gradually that nobody could point to the moment it happened.

She was still testing it, plucking and adjusting, when Adriano appeared with a water bottle for her, because he had noticed she skipped the break. "Mr. Hosseini is about to start the run-through," he said. "You'd better intervene before he counts us in, or he'll stop the whole orchestra and glare at everybody."

Rachel carried the violin to her seat just as Mr. Hosseini raised his baton. The long open A arrived, and this time she let it ring out steady and true, matching the cellos beneath her. Karina turned her head slightly and gave her a thumbs-up without missing her own part.

After the rehearsal, Mr. Hosseini stopped beside her chair. "Whatever you did at the break," he said, "keep doing it." On the way out, past the lobby where Adriano's propaganda poster for the history fair still hung, Rachel zipped her case and smiled at the sagging drawing of a string vibrating fast, which she intended to sketch the moment she got home. "Tomorrow," she told Karina, "I'm tuning every single string before my feet even hit the floor."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Delayed muscle soreness is not caused by lactic acid, which returns to normal levels within about an hour after exercise.
story:
Saturday practice at Riverside Park always smelled like cut grass and somebody's dog. Blake laced his cleats on the bench while Joe groaned and rubbed his thighs like they were made of wet cement.

"I can barely walk," Joe said. "It's all that lactic acid from yesterday's drills. Coach said so."

Blake tilted his head. "Yesterday's? We finished drills at five o'clock yesterday. It's ten in the morning now."

"So?"

"So if it was lactic acid, shouldn't it have worn off by now? I read that lactic acid goes back to normal within about an hour after exercise." Blake stood up and bounced on his toes. "Which means yesterday's practice can't be making you sore today. Something else is."

Joe squinted at him the way he did when Blake claimed the cafeteria's meatloaf came from a carnivore that had eaten too many cafeteria meatballs. "You made that up."

"Fine. Let's test it. After practice today, you check your legs every hour. If the lactic acid theory is right, you'll feel great by lunch tomorrow." Blake grinned. "If you're still sore, I win, and you carry my bag to the car for a week."

"Deal," Joe said, and they ran onto the field before Ms. Kapoor, who coached the team and also lived two houses down from Blake, could yell at them for being late.

Practice was long and muddy. Blake slipped once trying a fancy turn and landed flat on his back, which made Eden laugh so hard she had to sit down on the ball she was supposed to be dribbling. "Smooth," she called. "Real smooth." He got up covered in grass clippings, determined not to look vain about his failed move, and spent the rest of the hour passing simply and running hard.

That afternoon Joe texted: STILL SORE. NOT LACTIC ACID. Blake texted back a single trophy emoji. But he wanted to be sure, not just right, so on Sunday he tried something else. He did twenty slow, easy squats in his bedroom, hardly enough to sustain any real effort, and waited. No soreness that evening. Then Monday he did fifty fast ones in the park, sprinted to the fence and back twice, and by Tuesday morning his legs ached exactly like Joe's had, one whole day later. Same delay. Same soreness, arriving the day after the work, never during it.

At Tuesday practice he found Joe by the water bottles. "It's the delay that gives it away," Blake said. "Whatever makes us sore shows up a day late. Lactic acid doesn't hang around that long."

Joe hoisted Blake's bag onto his shoulder with a dramatic sigh. "Fine. Science boy. But you still owe me for that meatloaf theory."

"Two meatloaf theories," Eden said, jogging past. "I keep a list."

Blake chased her halfway to the goal.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Letting all the air out of the tube first makes the tyre loose enough to lever off the rim.
story:
Noah propped his bike against the window of the Spin Cycle Laundromat and knelt on the sidewalk, holding the flat front tyre up like evidence. His mom was inside folding towels, and his friend Lindsey sat on the counter beside the dryers, kicking her heels against the metal.

"Pop it off with the lever," Lindsey said, swinging her legs. "How hard can it be? You cited a whole video about this yesterday."

"I didn't cite it, I watched it," Noah said. "Three times." He slid the orange plastic lever under the edge of the tyre, pressed down, and nothing happened. He pressed harder. The lever bent, the tyre stayed glued to the rim, and his thumb slipped off and pinched a fold of skin. "Ow. Okay, the video guy made it look like butter."

Ms. Do, who ran the laundromat and was sweeping between the machines, leaned on her broom to watch. "That wheel's fighting you," she said cheerfully, and went back to her sweeping without offering a single helpful hint, which Noah felt was almost rude.

He sat back and stared at the tyre, thinking. When the guy in the video levered his off, the tyre had looked floppy, like a wet noodle. Noah's still looked round-ish, puffed a little near the valve, like a balloon three days after a birthday. He pinched the tyre. Squishy, but not noodly. Then, all at once, he had an idea, and it felt like finding the last puzzle piece under the couch. Maybe the lever would only work once every last bit of air was gone. He unscrewed the little valve cap, pressed the valve pin with the tip of a tyre lever, and listened to the faint, pathetic hiss until there was nothing left to hiss. The tyre went completely slack. He slid the lever under the edge again, pushed down, and the whole side of the tyre flopped over the rim so easily he nearly fell backward into the change machine.

"It worked!" Noah held up the lever like a trophy. Lindsey hopped off the counter to see.

She ran a finger along the inside of the tyre, checking for whatever had caused the puncture, and stopped. "Noah. Look." She pulled out a tiny plastic dinosaur, a green T. rex no bigger than a thumbnail, its little arms raised in triumph. "I think this was in the wash, and I think it escaped."

Ms. Do peered at it, then at the row of dryers, and smiled. "That's from the lost sock bag. Symmetry at last. One sock goes missing every week, and now something comes back out." Noah laughed, found the real culprit, a tiny thorn two spokes over, patched the tube, pumped the tyre until it was firm again, and dropped the T. rex into his shirt pocket, its little head poking out like a passenger.

"New mascot," he said. "He rides with me from now on."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid proved in his Elements that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
story:
Rain tapped the windows of Grandpa's house all morning, the kind of steady precipitation that made the whole room feel wrapped in cotton. Stella sat at the kitchen table with his old laptop, which emitted a faint hum and a smell of warm dust whenever it worked hard. She was writing her first real Python program, and Trace had bet her a milkshake it would take a week.

The program was supposed to ask for a number and say whether it was prime. Her first attempt had a bug: when she typed 9, it printed "prime," which was wrong, and she'd stared at the code until her eyes ached. Finally she noticed her loop stopped one number too early, so it never tested dividing by 3. She fixed it, and the machine, perfectly impartial, judged 9 as "not prime," then 11 as "prime," then 13 as "prime." She felt like she'd pulled a splinter out of her own thinking.

The rain kept falling while she typed bigger and bigger numbers. 97. 893. 7,919. All prime, all confirmed. She began to wonder about the biggest one, the final prime at the end of the line, the record-holder. If she found it, she could name it after herself. She was still thinking about that when Grandpa came in, shaking droplets off his cardigan, and set a cloth-bound book on the table beside her. It was his copy of Euclid's Elements, printed in Greek and English side by side, and she remembered the summer he'd tried to read it to her and she'd rolled her eyes and gone outside instead. She'd chosen the sprinkler over mathematics, and she wasn't sure she regretted it, but tonight she wished she'd listened.

"That guy proved something about my numbers?" she asked.

"Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many prime numbers," Grandpa said.

"Infinite?" Stella said it out loud, then laughed. Trace was going to lose the milkshake bet in more ways than one, because there was no biggest prime for her to find. There was only the next one. She bent over the keyboard, typed 10,007, and hit enter. The laptop hummed, the screen glowed, and one word appeared: prime.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
story:
Alexander had been to the cultural center before, for a Lunar New Year fair and once for a film night, but tonight the big hall was arranged with long tables and white cloths, and candles flickered down the whole length of them. His family found seats near his aunt and uncle, and across the table sat his cousin Miriam, who was seven and holding a folded paper so tightly it had gone soft at the creases. She had been practicing all week, his mom whispered, and every time she practiced she got a little quieter.

"Four Questions," Miriam's father said to her, patting her hand. "You'll be wonderful." Alexander leaned over to his friend Juliette, who had come along because her own family was curious about the holiday. "Do you know what those are?" she asked. He shook his head. He only knew that this meal, the Seder, retold the story of the Exodus, how the Israelites left Egypt, and that everyone at the table had a part in it.

The meal began with readings that went around the table, older voices and younger ones, and Mr. Lee, who ran the center, moved between the tables refilling water glasses. Then came the moment when the room went quiet and everyone looked at Miriam. She stood up. Her mouth opened, and nothing came out. Her eyes filled, and she sat back down so fast her chair scraped, which made a man at the next table glance over in a way that seemed to irritate her father.

Alexander thought about the pattern he had watched all evening. Every part of the Seder belonged to somebody, and the parts had an order, like categories: the readings, the food, the songs, the questions. The youngest able child asked the Four Questions. That was the rule. Not the oldest, not the loudest, not whoever volunteered. He tested the idea in his head: if he just stood up and read them himself, everyone would know it was wrong, because the part belonged to her, not to him. But able, he thought. There had to be a way to make her able.

He slid his chair over and whispered, "You know them better than me. I'll say the first line with you, then you take it." Miriam stared at him. "My voice shook at the spring concert," he told her. "In front of the whole school, in that big prestigious auditorium. It still came out okay." She stood up again, gripping the paper, and Alexander stood too, and said the opening words with her. Her voice was thin on the first line, steadier on the second, and by the fourth question she was alone, clear, and the whole hall listened.

When she finished, people banged the tables and called out, and Juliette whispered, "She did it." Miriam folded the paper into a tiny square and handed it to Alexander like a prize.

"Next year you won't need me," he said.

"Next year I still will," she said, "but only for the first line."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
story:
Lucy had a theory, and the theory was that Ms. Tan wrote the world's worst cursive. Every word on the whiteboard looked like it had been left out in the rain, smudged into grey worms. When Bree passed her a note asking what the homework was, Lucy squinted at the whiteboard, then at the note, and realized with an uncomfortable thud that the note was smudged too, even though her nose was practically touching it.

"Your eyes aren't broken," said Allegra at lunch, pushing up her own glasses. "You're just turning into me. It's genetic. Also contagious. You sat too close."

"Very funny." But Lucy kept thinking about it on the walk home. Allegra's glasses fixed far-away things, because Allegra's eyes were bad at distance. Lucy's eyes were bad at everything, near and far, which didn't fit. She decided to test it. She borrowed Allegra's glasses the next morning, held up her biology worksheet, and the letters wobbled worse, like they were underwater. So the Allegra theory was dead. Something else was going on, and she couldn't see it directly, which felt deeply unfair. The problem was inside her own eyes and invisible.

The optometrist's office smelled like plastic and peppermints. Lucy read the letters through a thing like a diving mask while the doctor flipped lenses, and suddenly the smallest line snapped into focus so sharply she laughed out loud. On the counter lay a plastic model of an eye, and beside it a pamphlet with a diagram: a round curve, then a curve shaped like an egg, longer one way than the other. "Astigmatism," Lucy read, and the picture made the whole thing click. Her cornea, that clear window at the front, was egg-shaped instead of round, curving more one direction than the other, so light bent unevenly and everything blurred, no matter how near or far. The new lenses would refract the light back into line.

"So it's not Ms. Tan's handwriting," Lucy said.

"It never was," said her dad from the corner, not even looking up from his magazine, which was its own kind of insult.

At home, Lucy put the glasses on and wandered the house like a tourist. She could see individual leaves on the tree outside. She could read the shampoo bottle. She turned on the television and found an ad for an influential glasses corporation, all sleek frames and dramatic music, and she struck a pose against the couch, copying the model's pout. Bree, sprawled on the rug, snorted so hard she choked on a cracker.

"Behold," Lucy announced, "the smudged no more."

"You're still the weirdest person I know," said Bree.

"And now I can see exactly how weird you are."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
The poster hung in the hallway of the community centre between the water fountain and the notice board, black and white, with a curly shape in the middle of it. Elena stopped in front of it on her way to the craft room, because Ralph and Ellia were already standing there, arguing.

"It's two faces," Ralph said. "Look, there's a nose, there's a chin. Two profiles staring at each other."

"It is not," said Ellia. "It's a vase. A fancy vase with a stem and everything. Are you looking at the same poster?"

Elena leaned closer. The moment she looked at the middle, she saw the vase, white and solid, sitting on a black background. Then she blinked, and somehow the white had split into two faces, and the vase was gone. She tried to hold both in her mind at once, the vase and the faces together, and it slipped away every time like water through her fingers. She wanted to know which one was really there, because both of them could not be, and neither of her friends would give in.

"Cover the bottom," she told Ellia. Ellia cupped her hands over the lower part of the poster, and Elena stared hard. "Faces," she announced. "Definitely faces."

"Now cover the sides," Elena said, and Ralph's palms hid the outer edges. This time the vase leapt out at her, clear and unmistakable.

"So who's right?" Ralph demanded.

"Both of us," Ellia said slowly. "And neither, kind of."

Below the poster hung a small white card, and Elena crouched to read it aloud. "The Rubin vase. Introduced by the Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915. It can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment."

"So we were never wrong," Ralph said. "We were just seeing it one at a time."

Elena straightened up, pleased with herself, as though she had managed to conquer a puzzle that had looked impossible from the start. Down the hall, Ms. Cho appeared with a frail old man on her arm, guiding him toward the pharmacy pickup window. A slip of paper fluttered from his coat pocket and landed near Elena's feet.

"Sir, your prescription," she called, and jogged over to hand it back. The old man smiled at her, and then at the poster over her shoulder.

"Two faces," he said.

Ellia laughed. "It's a vase," she said, and pointed at the white shape, and the three of them stood in the hallway trying to see it his way.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Rotating crops, so the same plant family is not grown in the same spot year after year, helps keep soil pests and diseases from building up.
story:
Grandma's tomato plants always stood in the same corner of the garden, right beside the fence, and this year they were failing. Samantha knelt in the dirt and turned over a yellowing leaf, then another, and counted six wilted stems before she reached the beans. The beans, two rows over, climbed their strings green and fat and cheerful. Something was wrong with that corner, but not with the whole garden.

"Your grandpa planted tomatoes there every single year," Grandma said, handing Samantha the watering can. "Thirty summers, maybe more."

Hallie, who had biked over to help, crouched down and poked the soil. "Maybe it's just bad dirt in that one spot."

"But the beans grew fine here last year," Samantha said, pointing to the row where the beans now stood. "And the year before, Grandpa said the peppers did well right there too. It's only sick where the tomatoes keep going." She drew a map in her notebook, one square for every year she could remember, and the pattern was hard to miss: tomato, tomato, tomato, always that corner, always sicker than the year before. Whatever was hurting them had to be building up, invisible, in that one patch of ground.

Samantha tested the idea the only way she could. She dug up the three healthiest tomato seedlings from the flat by the porch and planted them in the bean row, far from the corner, then put beans where the tomatoes had been. Denise came by on Saturday to see the experiment, and the results were still ambiguous: the transplanted tomatoes looked droopy from the move, and the corner beans hadn't sprouted. "This proves nothing," Denise said.

"Then we wait," Samantha said.

Three weeks later the waiting paid off. The transplanted tomatoes stood straight and put out new leaves, and the corner beans poked through in a crooked, stubborn line. Grandma laughed and called Samantha her little garden scientist, and when Mr. Kerr leaned over the fence to admire the beans, Samantha explained her plan. "Next year the tomatoes move again, and the year after that too. It's called rotating crops. The same plant family never goes in the same spot year after year." The sick old stems in the corner had dwindled to dry sticks, and she pulled them out one by one and dropped them in the compost bin, well away from the soil.

"Ordering seeds for spring?" Mr. Kerr asked.

"Already did," Samantha said, and held up her notebook, the map of next summer drawn fresh and clean.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Hinduism, moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth, and it is considered the highest goal of human life.
story:
Grayson set his laptop on the kitchen counter next to a box of cereal and a glass prism he had borrowed from the science shelf. On the screen was the assignment from Ms. Crowchild: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had picked Hinduism and Christianity because his grandmother was Hindu and Leana's family went to a church, which meant he could get his facts from actual people instead of just skimming websites. His poster board lay flat on the table, divided by a line drawn so carefully perpendicular to the edges that Liv, who had come over to help, checked it twice with a ruler.

"So what's the Christian side?" Liv asked, opening the marker box.

"Heaven. You live once, then you're judged, then heaven." Grayson wrote it in blue. "And for Hinduism I put rebirth, which sounds way better. You get to come back. If you mess up seventh grade, big deal, you try again as somebody else."

Liv scrutinize d his half-finished poster. "You wrote 'rebirth is the prize' in giant letters."

"Because it is," Grayson said.

Liv picked up his draft notes, then his mother's phone from the counter. "Ask your grandmother. You said you were going to call her anyway."

He dialed, and while the phone rang he held the prism up to the window so that sunlight split into a stripe of colors across the cereal box. His grandmother answered. He asked her straight out whether being reborn was something you hoped for or something you wanted to escape, and there was a pause long enough for him to worry the question was rude.

"Being reborn is the cycle, and we go around and around," she said. "Moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth, and it is the highest goal of human life."

Grayson wrote it down word for word. Then he looked at his poster, where "rebirth is the prize" stretched across half the board in letters the size of his hand. He had spent forty minutes on that lettering.

"So I had it backwards," he said. "Rebirth is more like the do-over, and the actual goal is getting out of the loop." He thought of it like the prism: one beam of light, but it broke into different colors depending on how you looked at it. Two faiths, one question, completely different pictures. He crossed out "prize," wrote "cycle," and moved his grandmother's quote to the top of the Hindu side in red.

Liv leaned over the poster with the ruler again. "You know your drawing looks like a Ferris wheel with arrows?"

"It's the cycle of rebirth," Grayson said, "and it's a great Ferris wheel."

When he got to class the next morning, Ms. Crowchild stopped at his desk, read the red quote, and asked where it came from. "My grandmother," Grayson said. "Primary source. Also she wants to know if she gets extra credit."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: In the Three Sisters method used by many Indigenous peoples of the Americas, corn supports climbing beans, and squash leaves shade the soil against weeds.
story:
The first thing Hunter planted on the balcony was corn, and the first thing that went wrong was the wind. It snapped two seedlings in a single night, and the survivors leaned against the railing like tired old men. He crouched beside the pots in the morning and tried to figure out what he had done to deserve this. Maybe the soil, maybe the watering, maybe nothing at all.

"Your beans look sad too," said Niam, who had climbed over from the next balcony the way he always did, without asking. The bean seedlings sprawled across the concrete in limp green tangles, reaching for nothing.

"I planted them to climb the corn," Hunter said. He pointed at the stalks. "They just don't seem to know it."

Ms. Cho, who kept tomato plants three balconies down, was watering her leaves and pretending not to listen, which meant she was about to stop pretending. She came over, sandals slapping, and studied the pots with her hands on her hips. "My grandmother planted this way," she said. "Corn, beans and squash all together. People call it the Three Sisters."

"The three what?"

"Sisters," she said, and went back to her tomatoes, offering nothing else, which was her way.

Hunter sat on the floor of the balcony and turned the phrase over. Three sisters. Sisters helped each other, didn't have to be told what to do. He thought of last summer, when he had begged his dad for a seed kit and then abandoned it in July when nothing sprouted fast enough. He had quit on things before. He did not want this to be another one of those stories he told himself later. So he tried an experiment. He redistributed the pots, distributing the beans so each one stood at the base of a cornstalk, then set a wide pot of squash between them, its broad leaves spread flat across the soil like a green quilt.

Niam came back a week later and stood at the railing with a popsicle, dripping orange onto the concrete. "Whoa," he said. The beans had found the corn on their own, curling upward in tight spirals, and where one stalk had wobbled in the wind the bean vine now held it steady. Under the squash leaves, the soil stayed dark and damp, and the weeds that had crowded every other pot on the balcony were simply absent. Hunter brushed his hand over the leaves. They felt cool and slightly rough, and the whole arrangement worked like a little guild, each plant holding up its end.

"It's like they planned it," Niam said.

"They kind of did," Hunter said, and he felt buoyant in a way he hadn't all spring. He was already measuring the empty corner of the balcony with his eyes, calculating how many more pots would fit before his mom noticed. "Next year we add a second bed."

"Where?"

Hunter tapped the concrete beside the door. "Right there," he said.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
story:
Georgia had one job at the cultural festival: run the Spanish club's booth for twenty minutes while Ms. Delgado took a break. She had practiced her sentences all week, and she was ready, except that Wesley kept hovering at her elbow.

"Ask me something in Spanish," she said. "Full sentences. Watch this. Mi hermano es alto. Mi perro es blanco. Mi hermana está cansada."

Wesley leaned in. "Okay, but why did you say es one time and está the other? You said them different."

The question landed harder than Wesley meant it to. Georgia remembered Tuesday night at the kitchen table, when she had written Mi hermano está alto on her practice sheet and her older brother had glanced over and burst out laughing. "You just said I'm temporarily tall," he'd said, wiping his eyes. "Like I'm only tall right now, and tomorrow I'll shrink." She had crossed it out and copied es instead without understanding why, and it had bugged her ever since.

She looked at her sentences again. Alto, blanco, cansado. Tall, white, tired. She tapped the page. "Okay, a hypothetical," she said. "If my brother got a good night's sleep, would he still be tall?" Wesley nodded slowly. "And would he still be tired?" Wesley shook his head, and then his eyes went wide. "Tired goes away. Tall doesn't."

"So maybe that's the rule," Georgia said. She tried it out loud. "Mi hermano es alto, because he's always tall. Mi hermana está cansada, because she's tired right now, and tomorrow she won't be." She said it twice more, and the words stopped feeling random. "Mi hermano es alto means he is tall," she added, "and Mi hermano está cansado means he is tired." The whole thing pivoted on whether the trait lasted.

Emmet arrived from the food line holding two churros, and he had his own agenda. "Tell me this means I get to write the booth sign," he said. He'd been angling for the sign all week because his handwriting was better than everyone's, and at first Georgia had said no, since the sentences were hers. Now she made up her mind and slid the marker across the table to him. "You do the letters, I'll tell you what to write. And I'm going to test it on Ms. Delgado before she's back."

When Ms. Delgado returned, Georgia stood up straight. "Mi hermano está cansado," she said carefully, watching her teacher's face. Ms. Delgado raised an eyebrow, then smiled and answered in English. "He should take a nap, then." Georgia grinned. Es for what stays, está for what doesn't. Wesley pumped his fist behind the churros.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
story:
Antoine sat on his bedroom floor with his goalkeeper gloves stretched over his fists, pulling at the elastic wristband until it snapped back. Tomorrow was the tryout, and Coach had already told the group that the final test would be facing penalty shots in front of everyone.

"Are you even listening?" Jackson said from the laptop screen. "I need you on my team. If you don't make it, I'm stuck with a keeper who watches the ball like it's going to bite him."

"I'm listening," Antoine said. "I just can't stop picturing everyone staring at me while I let in five shots in a row."

"That's stress," Jackson said. "My mom calls it that. I get it before every math test."

Antoine had heard Ms. Eze, his neighbour, use the word too, along with another one, anxiety, when she talked about feeling wound up before big moments. She'd said something once about how her doctor taught her a way to cope. Antoine tried to remember it while his heart thumped just from imagining the tryout. He closed his eyes. He could not recall her words exactly, but he remembered her sitting on her porch, breathing in through her nose and letting the air out in one long, slow stream, like she was cooling a bowl of soup.

He tried it. In through the nose, then a slow exhale, longer than the breath in. He counted and did it four times. His heart still beat, but slower, and his shoulders dropped an inch.

"Did you just fall asleep?" Jackson asked.

"No. Slow breathing with long exhales. It's a coping skill, Ms. Eze calls it that. You do it before a stressful moment, and it calms your body down."

"That's what goalies do," Jackson said. "I saw it in a highlights video. The keeper takes a big slow breath out right before the penalty kick."

They tested it. Antoine set up a rolled sock as the ball and Jackson counted as a fake crowd over the speaker, shouting "Antoine! Antoine!" at full volume. The first time, Antoine laughed and lost count. The second time, he took his slow breath with the long exhale, and when Jackson yelled "shot," his hands were already moving toward the sock. He caught it clean.

"Again," he said.

They ran it six more times, and he caught four. Then Jackson went quiet in a way Antoine recognized.

"Jackson. What's wrong?"

"Nothing."

"You did your test-face."

Jackson sighed into the microphone. "Fine. I'm trying out too, and I'm terrible at penalties. I've been dodging extra practice all week. Every time my dad says let's shoot some, I evade him. Today he found me hiding behind the garage."

Antoine grinned. "You're like a bad diplomat. You keep promising peace talks and then avoiding the meeting."

"Ha ha."

"Try it. The breathing. Before you take a shot."

"That's for keepers."

"So? Stress is stress. Breathe out slow, then shoot."

Jackson went silent, and Antoine could hear him inhale, then release one long audible breath across the microphone. "Okay," Jackson said. "Meet me at the field at eight. You bring the balls. I'll bring my dad."

Antoine pulled the gloves off and set them by the door, ready. "Eight sharp," he said, and gave the wristband one last snap.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives a steady base, so the onion cannot roll while you slice it.
story:
Mr. Holloway's kitchen smelled of garlic and warm tomatoes, and Bennett stood at the steel counter with an apron tied twice around his waist because it was sized for a grown man. He had wanted this Saturday job ever since his class toured the restaurant in September, and today was his first real lesson: onion, knife, sauce from scratch. Felix had come along too, mostly because Felix wanted to ask Mr. Holloway for a job washing dishes, and he kept hovering near the sink as if standing there long enough would make him official.

"Claw grip," Mr. Holloway said, curling his fingers so the knuckles stuck out like a guard rail, the fingertips tucked safely behind. "Knuckles guide the blade. Fingertips never come out to play." He handed Bennett a whole onion and a sharp knife, then went to check the simmering pot.

Bennett set the onion on the cutting board and laid the blade against its round side. The onion rolled. He caught it, tried again, and it rolled again, sliding right off the board and onto the floor with a soft thud. Felix snickered from the sink. "That's it, I'm boycotting onions," Felix announced. "They fight back."

Bennett picked the onion up and turned it over in his hand, thinking. The thing was round on every side, so it rolled no matter where he set it, which felt arbitrary and unfair, like a rule invented to ruin his morning. But the rule had to have a way around it. He looked at the onion's pointy top and the little root tuft at the other end. If he cut it in half from top to root, each half would have a flat side, and a flat side down meant the onion could not roll while he sliced it. He lined up the knife and cut down through the top, through the middle, all the way to the root. Two halves. He laid one flat side down on the board and touched it with a fingertip. Steady as a brick.

"Oh," said Felix, watching. "Flat side down. That's smart." He drifted over from the sink, his dishwashing campaign forgotten for the moment.

Bennett curled his hand into the claw, knuckles forward, and sliced slowly. The half stayed put the whole time, and the pile of even crescents grew under his blade. Mr. Holloway came back, looked at the board, and nodded once. "Onions in the pan when you're ready," he said. "And you," he added, glancing at Felix, "there are dishes in the rack if you're serious." Felix was already rolling up his sleeves. Bennett swept the chopped onion into his palm and held it over the hissing pan, then let the pieces fall.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many others are watching, because each person assumes someone else will act.
story:
The lemonade glass sweated in Hailey's hand while her grandfather searched the drawer for the rubber bands he swore he had left there. Outside, Mr. Lavoie was negotiating with a squirrel over his tomato plants, and losing. Hailey wasn't really watching either of them. She was thinking about Thursday, when Logan had mimicked the way Naomie's voice cracked during her book report, and the whole back row had laughed, and Hailey had stared at her desk as if there were something fascinating on it.

"Grandpa, can I ask you something?" she said. "If a bunch of people watch something bad happen and nobody does anything, does that mean they're all jerks?"

He stopped rummaging and settled onto the stool across from her, which took a while because his knees announced every movement. "Funny you should ask. When I was about your age, a kid got knocked into the creek at a church picnic. Forty of us standing around, and nobody jumped in. Not one." He shook his head. "Later I read about it. Psychologists call it the bystander effect. The more people watching, the less likely any one person is to help, because everyone figures somebody else will do it."

"So it's not that they're jerks?"

"It's not that they're off the hook, either," Grandpa said. "But I'll tell you, nobody at that picnic felt like a coward. Every single one of us felt like a person waiting for a braver person to show up."

Hailey turned that over. Forty people, and it had felt to each of them like an empty room. On Thursday there had been maybe six watchers, and she had still let Briana's elbow and Logan's smirk and Naomie's red ears convey the whole message to her: stay out of it. She had even told herself she was "not making it worse." That was the part that made her stomach hurt now, the smooth way she'd dressed up doing nothing.

Briana had called her that night, and they'd agreed, in a shaky truce, that they'd both been terrible, and then changed the subject to the dance. Briana wanted to forget it. Hailey couldn't, quite.

"Here's what I don't get," she said. "If everyone's waiting for someone else, then the fix is just... being the someone."

Grandpa smiled like she'd finally found the rubber bands, which she had; they were in the junk drawer all along. "That's the fix. It's also the hard part."

Monday, when Logan started up again about Naomie's voice, Hailey stood up so fast her chair squeaked against the floor. "You already did that joke. It was weak the first time." The room went quiet, and then Briana, to her visible surprise at herself, said, "Yeah, it was."

Naomie looked over at them. Mr. Lavoie would have called it a small harvest, but it was a start.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: A thicker wire of the same material and length has less resistance than a thinner one, because current has more room to flow.
story:
Clara clipped the thin wire into the circuit and squinted at the multimeter. "Two point eight volts," she read aloud, "and zero point four amps." She did the division on her notepad, twice, because the answer seemed wrong. Seven ohms. That was almost twice what the thick wire had given them.

"That can't be right," Sylas said, peering over her shoulder. "It's the same length and the same stuff. It should be the same." He tapped the coil of thin wire as if the number might fall out of it.

Ms. Boateng, their neighbour, had lent them the whole setup from her garage, but she had refused to say anything else. "You can extract the answer yourselves," she had said at the fence, handing over the meter. "Measure the voltage, measure the current, divide. That's all I'll tell you." Clara had thought that was unfair at first. Now she wondered if the old meter was simply broken.

"Let's test it," Clara said. She unclipped the thin wire and put the thick one back in its place, then turned the knob slowly. Bodie, who had been lying in the grass watching a beetle, sat up and held the leads steady. The needle settled. Two point eight volts, zero point seven amps. Four ohms. Clara wrote it down and looked at the two numbers side by side, the same voltage each time, different current. Something about the wires themselves was changing the answer, something she couldn't see. She held the thin wire up to the light, then the thick one, and turned them slowly between her fingers.

"Same length," she said. "Same material. The only difference is that this one is skinny and this one is fat." She thought about the crowded hallway at school, how the whole class moved faster when they could spread out into two doors instead of squeezing through one. "I think a thicker wire of the same material and length has less resistance. That's why more current got through." Sylas frowned at his notepad, where he had already written "broken meter" and underlined it. He crossed it out with one slow line.

"So my theory is dead," he said, but he was almost smiling. "Is it feasible to test a middle-sized one? Because I bet it lands between four and seven."

Clara dug through the box of supplies and pulled out a wire that was neither thick nor thin. "Then we're an alliance again," she said, clipping it in. "Hold the leads steady, Bodie." She turned the knob and leaned close to the dial.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running the second half of a race faster than the first is called a negative split; running the first half faster is called a positive split.
story:
Christopher had blown the eight hundred metres twice already. Both times he sprinted the first lap like it was a hundred, led the field into the second lap, and then watched three runners pass him before the finish. Today, in the school gym, Mr. Crowchild had set up the oval of cones around the basketball lines for indoor practice, and Christopher intended to figure the race out.

The problem was the pace itself. He could not see it. If he went too fast, his legs turned heavy in the second lap, but he had no way to know he had gone too fast until it was too late. He borrowed his mother's watch, which had a heart-rate sensor on the underside, and clipped it on before warm-up. The sensor couldn't tell him his lap times, but it could tell him whether his body was already working too hard halfway through the first lap. That was something he could test.

Zak and Luca were running the practice race with him. Before they started, Luca handed him a folded note, torn from a math worksheet. "Zak wrote down his times from Saturday," Luca said. "He wants you to see them." The note read: "Lap 1: 62 seconds. Lap 2: 75 seconds. I died. What happened?" Christopher stared at the two numbers. Zak had gone out fast and finished slow, exactly like him. The direction of the two laps, fast then slow, was the pattern. So the answer was to run it backwards.

"Zak," Christopher called across the gym, "when your second lap is faster than your first, that's called a negative split."

"Then mine was a positive split," Zak said, looking at the note. "Fast then slow. Great."

Mr. Crowchild supervised from the bleachers, whistle in his mouth, and said nothing about pacing. He only checked that nobody cut inside the cones. When he blew the whistle, Christopher ran the first lap deliberately behind Zak and Luca, watching the number on the sensor's screen. It climbed but stayed below where it had been in his failed races, so he held that effort even though it felt embarrassingly slow.

At the start of the second lap, with his legs still under him, he moved up alongside Zak. The finish felt imminent, only two hundred metres away, and Christopher pushed hard through the last curve. He crossed the line first, and Luca was already shouting the times. "Sixty-eight and sixty-four! You went faster at the end!" Zak bent over, hands on his knees, then straightened up and pointed at Christopher's watch.

"Show me how to set that sensor," he said.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
story:
The rink smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee, and Oliver laced his skates with his English homework still rattling around his head. He was supposed to be writing about the antagonist of his book, a squirrel named Reginald who stole acorns, but every time he tried to think about Reginald, his stomach flipped instead. Hockey tryouts started in twenty minutes, and there were only three spots on the school team.

A girl sat two benches down, taping her stick. Oliver had seen her at the public rink before, quick and low, better on edges than half the boys who had showed up today. Malcolm leaned over and whispered, "They're going to cut her in the first five minutes. Coach hates this."

"Cut her for what? She skates better than Frank."

"For being a girl, genius," Malcolm said. "Team's always been boys."

That was when Frank skidded up, breathless, holding a folded page he'd pulled off the corkboard by the office. "You have to see this. The athletic director posted it. It's a law. Title IX, signed in 1972. It bans discrimination based on sex in schools that get federal money, and it's been applied to their sports programs. So she can try out. She has to be allowed to."

Oliver read it twice. The words were plain, but the effect was strange, like finding out the rink had a door he'd never noticed. He thought about last year, when his mother had asked if he wanted to sign up for figure skating lessons and he'd said no because hockey felt like the thing that was done. What was that about, really? He wasn't sure yet, and he filed the question away.

The girl came out on the ice anyway, before anyone could argue, and in the first drill she took the puck off Malcolm so cleanly he spun a full circle and sat down hard on the volatile surface, which for the record was not the ice's fault. Coach blew the whistle. Nobody laughed at Malcolm, mostly because everyone was watching her thread the cone line.

She ended up on Oliver's line for the scrimmage. He passed to her, mostly because she was open, partly because Reginald the antagonist would not have passed, and Oliver wanted to be a different kind of character than that. The winning goal was hers, off his rebound, and afterward she tapped his helmet with her stick.

Malcolm limped over, rubbing his hip. "Okay," he said. "She's terrifying and I want her on my team forever."

"Then say that to the coach," Oliver said, "before he posts anything else on that corkboard."

Frank was already skating toward the bench, waving the folded page over his head like it could symbolize something, which, Oliver thought, maybe it did.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
story:
Layla stood in front of the washing machine with her mother's note in one hand: sort the darks, check the pockets, one capful of detergent, cold water. It was her first solo load, and she wanted it perfect because her mother had left her in charge of laundry for the whole weekend.

She sorted fast, tossing jeans and black shirts and her navy hoodie into the drum. Check the pockets, the note said, but she was already behind, because Calvin and Maggie were coming over at two. She patted a few pockets, found nothing, and dumped in the rest.

An hour later she opened the dryer and froze. Every dark item was speckled with white. Her favourite hoodie looked like it had been caught in a snowstorm, and when she shook it, tiny shreds drifted down like dust. Layla held up a pair of jeans and stared. Something had gone wrong, but the machine was clean and the detergent was the right one. She thought about her grandmother, who used to say "check the pockets" in that voice that meant she had learned the hard way. Layla had thought it was about losing money or keys.

She dug through the warm clothes and found the culprit: a crumpled paper tissue, or what was left of one, wedged in the pocket of her black shorts. One tissue had broken apart in the wash and scattered shreds over everything else in the drum. That was why people checked pockets before washing, she realized, not for the tissue's sake but for the clothes'. She felt a flash of guilt about rushing, and a smaller, defiant flash that insisted nobody had told her tissues did this.
