She tested her idea before despairing. She rolled tape around her hand, sticky side out, and pressed it over the speckled hoodie, lifting shreds away in little grey clumps. Then she tried a damp cloth, dragging it across the jeans, which seemed to distribute the remaining bits into the fabric instead of removing them. Tape was better. She worked through the load piece by piece, and when the doorbell rang at two, the hoodie was almost clean.

"You look like you fought a pillow," Calvin said from the doorway.

"It was a tissue," Layla said, holding up the tape-covered hand like evidence. "One tissue. It's a paradox, kind of. Something soft turned into the biggest mess of my whole weekend."

Maggie peered at the pile of dark clothes. "Are they ruined?"

Layla picked up the hoodie and shook it once, hard, watching for white dust in the light. Nothing fell. "Almost not," she said.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and wet raincoats, and Emmett was holding his new phone like it might dissolve. His dad had handed it over that morning with a list of rules, and rule number one, taped to the box, said he had to set up every account before dinner tonight. He was tapping through the screens when a message popped up that made his stomach drop: a code, six digits, for an account login he had never asked for.

"Whoa, wait," said Lara, leaning over from the seat beside him. "You just got that? You didn't type anything?" Sylas turned around from the row ahead, his backpack sliding into the aisle. The bus hissed to a stop at Maple Street, and somewhere behind them a kindergartner dropped a juice box.

"No," Emmett said slowly. "I was just setting up my email. This is a login code for my game account." He stared at it. Somebody had typed his password somewhere. Somebody who was not him. The thought made the back of his neck prickle, because his password was the same three words he used for everything, including the email he had just made.

"Maybe it's a glitch," Sylas offered. Lara looked skeptical. "My brother says glitches don't guess your password," she said. "Somebody knows it. That's why they can even get to the part where they need the code."

Emmett turned that over. The code was the thing standing between the stranger and his account. Without the code, they couldn't get in, even with the password. His dad had called it something on the drive to school this morning, a phrase Emmett had half ignored. "Two-factor authentication," he said out loud, testing it. Lara nodded. "That's what the sign-in screen calls it. It asks for a second proof, like a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in."

"So right now," Emmett said, "they're stuck at the code screen." He checked the clock on the bus dashboard. Fourteen minutes until they reached school, and his free period after lunch was the only time the library computers were open before the deadline. First move, though, he could do right here. He went into the game's settings, changed the password to something long and strange, and typed it twice without looking up. Then he found the switch labeled two-factor authentication and turned it on. A test code buzzed into his palm, proof that it worked.

At lunch he and Lara sat at the corner computer and checked the account history. Three failed login attempts from a city two states away, all that morning, all stopped at the code screen. "They tried before I changed it," Emmett said. "They'll try again." He scrolled through his other accounts and made a list of candidates for the same weak password: the library app, the science homework site, the club schedule page. One by one he opened each one. Two still used the old password, and he fixed both while Lara read the codes out loud as they arrived, her finger tracing the screen so he didn't lose his place.

By the time the bell rang, the list had diminished to nothing. Sylas appeared at the door with his backpack on one shoulder. "So the mystery hacker?" he asked. Emmett held up the phone, showing the account screen, all green checks, no new codes all afternoon. "Locked out," he said. "Every door, every lock."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen.
story:
Benjamin lined up five glasses on the kitchen counter: lemon juice, soapy water, milk, vinegar, and baking soda mixed with water. He had saved two weeks of allowance for the little packet of litmus paper, and today he was finally going to test everything in the kitchen like a real chemist.

"We should do the mystery glass," said Leyla, who had come over with her backpack still on. "My uncle works at a museum, and he transports old science equipment in a padded van. He says the real scientists test things that are unknown, not things where you already know the answer."

Aksil, who had arrived five minutes late and out of breath, held up a glass of cloudy liquid he had brought from home. "This is my mystery liquid. My grandma's old recipe. If you're such a scientist, tell me what's in it." He grinned, but his hands were tight around the glass, like the answer mattered to him.

Benjamin tore off a strip of red litmus paper and dipped it into the lemon juice. Nothing happened. He dipped a blue strip into the same glass, and the paper turned pink. "Acid," he announced. "Acids turn blue litmus red. Bases turn red litmus blue." He moved down the line, dropping wet strips onto a paper towel. Soap turned the red strip blue. Vinegar was an acid like the lemon juice. Milk barely did anything at all, which made him frown and write a question mark in his notebook.

Then he dipped both strips into Aksil's mystery glass. The blue strip stayed blue, and the red strip slowly, lazily turned blue too. "Base," said Benjamin. "Your grandma's recipe has something like soap or baking soda in it." Aksil's face fell. "It's supposed to be lemonade," he admitted. "I think the powder I used was baking soda, not lemonade mix." Leyla laughed so hard she had to sit down on the kitchen floor.

"That's the pH scale doing its job," said Ms. Bear, their neighbor, who had knocked to return a casserole dish and now stood in the doorway watching. "Do you know who came up with that scale?" Aksil immediately said, "Some English guy, obviously." Benjamin said he thought it was a French scientist, because so much chemistry sounded French.

Leyla pulled out her phone and scrolled to a photo she had taken at her uncle's museum, a placard beside a display of old glass jars. She held it out. The placard read that the pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen. "Danish," said Benjamin slowly. "And at a beer laboratory. That's like a whole guild of chemists working on brewing." Ms. Bear smiled and set the casserole dish on the counter.

"So his scale is still what we just used," Benjamin said, tapping his notebook. "A hundred years old and still working in my kitchen." He wrote the date at the top of his results page, then tore off two fresh strips. "Okay, Aksil. Go home, get the real lemonade mix, and bring it back. We'll test that too."

"Deal," said Aksil, and he was out the door before Benjamin could cap the vinegar.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
story:
Leo had the best seat in the living room, the corner of the couch where the cushion was worn exactly to his shape, and he was not giving it up. His dad was in the recliner, Rudy and Tenley were squeezed onto the floor pillows, and Ms. Haddad from next door had planted herself on the armchair with a bowl of popcorn balanced on her knee like it was a crown. The big game filled the television, and the crowd noise roared out of the speakers so loud that the pictures on the wall shivered.

"Come on, come on!" Rudy shouted, leaping up when the home team's receiver dropped a pass in the end zone. "The whole stadium was willing him to catch it and he still blew it!"

"That's the humiliation of playing at home," Tenley said, shaking her head. "You've got eighty thousand people screaming for you and you still drop the ball."

Leo frowned at the screen. He had been thinking about something all afternoon, and now it pushed its way out. "Wait. Does screaming actually help, though? Like, at all?"

Everyone turned to look at him. His dad pointed a chip at the TV. "Of course it helps. Home field advantage. Everybody knows that. The crowd lifts the team."

"Did you monitor the score just now, though?" Leo said. "We yelled the loudest on that last drive and they still lost five yards." He pulled out the tablet his mom kept by the couch and started typing while Tenley leaned over his shoulder, stealing popcorn. He was looking for proof, one way or the other, that all this noise did something.

"Here it is," he said a minute later. His eyes went wide. "Okay, so in the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1. That's basically dead even. No home advantage at all."

"Wait." Tenley grabbed the tablet. "One hundred twenty-seven wins, one hundred twenty-eight losses, and one tie? That's nothing. That's a coin flip."

"So the cheering," Rudy said slowly, "did nothing? All those years I screamed at the television for nothing?"

"The yelling was for you, not for them," Ms. Haddad said, and popped a kernel into her mouth.

Leo decided to test it. He stood on the couch, put both hands beside his mouth, and bellowed, "DO THE OPPOSITE OF WHATEVER YOU WERE GOING TO DO!" The dog fled under the coffee table. His dad fell off the recliner laughing, and the couch cushion, no longer held down by Leo's weight, flipped up perpendicular to the seat like a drawbridge.

On the next play, the home team ran the ball forty yards for a touchdown.

Rudy pointed at Leo with a trembling chip. "He did that. Leo, do it again. Do the opposite of what you did."

Leo climbed down, straightened the cushion, and cleared his throat. "I can't," he said. "That would be the same as doing it, and I'd have to do the opposite of that, and we'd be here all night." He grabbed the last handful of popcorn. "Somebody else yell something backwards."

Tenley spun to face the television, took an enormous breath, and hollered, "NOS! NOS! NOS!"

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun also gets longer days, giving sunlight more hours to warm the ground.
story:
"Bedtime at nine? But it's still light out!" Hayden stared at his grandpa, who only pointed at the clock on the porch wall.

Last summer at camp it had been the same. Hayden flashed back to the night he'd lay on his bunk watching the sky stay pale through the cabin window while the counselor shouted "Lights out!" from the door. Everyone else groaned about the lake water being cold, but Hayden had been stuck on a different puzzle: how could it be dark at nine in December and bright at nine in June? He'd had no answer then. He had a whole week at Grandpa's now, and no bedtime until he found one.

He called Emerick, who lived next door to Grandpa, and by suppertime Emerick and Gerald were both on the porch with a flashlight, an orange, and a knitting needle Grandpa dug out of a drawer. Hayden pushed the needle straight through the orange. "The orange is Earth. The needle is the axis. Now tilt it." He adjusted the angle until the top half of the orange leaned toward the flashlight, which Gerald held perfectly still. When Hayden spun the orange slowly, they counted how much of the top half stayed in the light. Almost all of it. The top half spent more time lit up on every turn, like a longer day.

"Now watch the bottom." Hayden spun it again, and the bottom half caught light only briefly, like a short day. "So the half tilted toward the flashlight gets longer days," he said. "And it works for the real Sun too. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets longer days, so sunlight has more hours to warm the ground. That's summer." Gerald leaned in so close his nose nearly touched the orange. "And the bottom half at the same time?" "Short days, less warming. Winter. The two halves are opposites." Hayden marked the top with a pen dot to keep his place, then spun it one more time to be sure.

Mr. Tang, the neighbour from across the road, had wandered over with his watering can and watched the whole experiment without a word. "Go on then," he said at last. "Show me June." Hayden tilted the orange the other way and gave the flashlight a solemn nod, as though taking testimony in court. "In June the bottom half leans toward the Sun, so they get summer down there while we get winter."

That night at nine the sky was still glowing pink over the fields. Hayden stood at his window, and even though Grandpa called lights out, he was smiling as he switched off the lamp. "Long day," he whispered to the bright window, "long day."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself.
story:
Hunter's grandfather kept an old laptop on the shelf under the crossword books, and on rainy afternoons Hunter was allowed to use it. Today he had a plan. His coding club was meeting tomorrow at Ms. Marino's classroom, and he wanted to walk in with a working program: one that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime.

He typed while his grandfather read the paper across the room. The program asked for a number, then tried dividing it by every number from two up to the number itself, checking for a remainder of zero. If nothing divided evenly, the number was prime. He tested it on 7, then 11. Both came back prime. His chest went tight with pride, and he called his friend Olivier right there in the kitchen to brag.

"Try nine," Olivier said over the phone. There was a smile hiding in his voice, and Hunter didn't like it.

He hung up, typed 9, and hit enter. PRIME, the screen said. Hunter frowned. Something was wrong, but he couldn't see it. The program was just words on a screen; the problem, whatever it was, sat inside it somewhere, invisible. He read the code line by line, then again, slower.

At coding club the next day, the argument was still going. Connor insisted nine was prime because it looked like it, all odd and solid. Olivier kept saying "try mine on the calculator" without explaining. Ms. Marino walked past their table but said nothing, only raised an eyebrow, which meant she wanted them to figure it out themselves. A note circulated through the club, passed hand to hand: Hunter's printout of his result, PRIME, with a question mark beside it in Olivier's handwriting.

Hunter spread the paper flat and thought about what a prime actually was. "A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself," he said slowly, testing the words. Then he picked up a pencil and divided 9 by 3. It came out even, no remainder. Three was a divisor, and three was not 1 and not 9. He looked up. "Nine isn't prime. And my program's wrong."

Back at his grandfather's house that evening, he stared at the code one more time. There, in the loop, he found it: he had told the program to divide by every number up to the number itself, but he had skipped the number 3 entirely, jumping from 2 to 4 because of a mistyped line. One small amendment, one letter changed, and he ran it again. He typed 9 and held his breath.

NOT PRIME, the screen said.

"Come look at this," he called to his grandfather, who shuffled over and read the screen through his glasses. "I have no idea what it means," the old man admitted, "but you look quite eloquent sitting there." Hunter grinned and typed 9 one more time, just to watch it print again.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
John spread six bean pots across the kitchen table and counted them twice, because the fair was in nine days and he had already lost one afternoon to a watering mix-up. Axel sat across from him, spinning a pencil.

"So which one gets the fancy fertilizer?" Axel asked.

"These three," John said, tapping the pots he had marked A, B, and C with masking tape. "Small dose, medium dose, big dose."

"And these two?"

"Plain water only. Nothing else."

Axel frowned. "Then why grow them at all? You're not testing them."

"I am, sort of. They're what I compare the others to." John paused, because until he said it out loud he hadn't realized how shaky that sounded. "If the fertilizer plants get tall, I need to know how tall they'd get anyway."

Axel still looked unconvinced, so John grabbed his notebook and drew a line down the middle. On the left he wrote "just water" and on the right "fertilizer." His little sister wandered through in her kangaroo pajamas, and Axel pointed at her and said, "Look, a marsupial," which made her growl and hop away. John laughed, but his eyes stayed on the notebook. He wrote a heading over the water pots: Control Group.

The next morning the trouble started. Pot B, the medium dose, looked droopy. Pot C looked worse. John stood at the table with his cereal going cold and turned the pots around, checking the soil, the leaves, the tape labels. If the fertilized plants were wilting while the plain water pots stood firm, then the fertilizer might actually be hurting them. But there was another possibility, and it bugged him all through breakfast: maybe all the plants were drooping because his room ran cold at night, and the fertilizer had nothing to do with it.

He checked the two control pots. Both stood straight, leaves out like little green hands.

That settled it. The droop belonged to the fertilizer, not the room. Without those untouched pots he would have had no way to know, and he might have abandoned the whole project and started over on something dull, like which paper towel holds the most water.

By Friday the medium-dose plant had recovered and pushed past the controls by four centimeters. The big dose still looked rough. John measured everything, then texted Axel: come over, bring your ruler, also your mom's phone has the good camera.

Axel arrived with both, plus a printout of a luminous jellyfish for reasons he never explained. They photographed the six pots in a row on the kitchen table, controls first, and Axel held the jellyfish picture out of frame.

"Good news," John said, arranging the ruler beside the tallest stem. "Plain water wins for looks, fertilizer wins for height. We've got ourselves a real result." He clicked the camera, and on the screen the little plant stood sharp and green, taller than everything behind it.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
The group chat had been pinging all afternoon, and Brooklyn could tell from the rhythm alone that something was wrong. Sarina always typed in short bursts, one thought per message, but today her messages came in long walls of text with no capitals. "guys I deleted it," she wrote. "the video is gone from my page, it's gone, stop bringing it up." The video had shown Sarina attempting a kickflip and instead planting her face into a recycling bin while a mushroom-looking fungus wobbled on the bin's lid, and half the grade had already seen it. Brooklyn noticed something else, too: in a group chat, everyone talks the same loud way, but in a private message people whisper. She slid into Sarina's DMs to test that idea. "are you actually okay or just saying that," she typed, and the three dots that appeared lasted almost a full minute before Sarina answered, "not okay."

Sarina's want was simple: she wanted the video erased from the earth. "If I delete it," she said aloud later at Mr. Sinclair's house, where the two of them fed his turtles every Wednesday for five dollars, "nobody can ever see it again, right?" Mr. Sinclair was sorting crickets into a cup and didn't even look up. "Ask the Wayback Machine," he said. "It's called the Wayback Machine," he added, when Brooklyn squinted at him. He would say nothing else about it, which was annoying, but also kind of thrilling, like being handed a locked box.

That night Brooklyn opened her laptop and typed the words in. A search bar. She pasted in the link to Sarina's page and hit the button. A calendar bloomed on the screen with little green marks, and when she clicked the month the video went up, there was the whole page, captured exactly as it had been, fungus, recycling bin, caption and all. She read the number at the top of the site twice because it seemed impossible: the Wayback Machine had saved more than one trillion web pages. A trillion. She sat with that for a second, wondering whether the internet was more like a library or like a fungus itself, quietly spreading copies of everything into places nobody checked.

"So it's still out there," Sarina said flatly when Brooklyn showed her the screen the next morning. "Even though I deleted it. Great. Wonderful. My face-plant is in a trillion-page museum." Her hopes of total erasure dwindled visibly, like the last popcorn in a shared bowl.

"Wait," Brooklyn said slowly. "Look at where the link points. The old page only loads if someone already knows the address and thinks to search for it." She refreshed Sar's live page, then the archived one, comparing them side by side. The archived copy had captured the video link, but the video file itself showed only a gray rectangle and the word "unavailable." Sarina lunged across the couch and hugged her so hard the laptop nearly slid to the floor.

"The bin ate the footage," Sarina announced to the group chat, with seventeen exclamation points. Naya replied with a single eye emoji, and Brooklyn laughed until her sides hurt, still wondering how many other deleted things were sitting quietly in that trillion-page pile, waiting for somebody curious enough to look.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: In 1837, ornithologist John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches.
story:
Aurora pressed her nose to the window of Mr. Kim's classroom and pointed at the bird feeder on the fence. "That's a wren," she said. "See the little curved beak."

Jaydon leaned over her shoulder. "That bird is the size of a potato. Wrens are tiny."

"It's a blackbird, then," Aurora said, and the bird, as if offended, flew off.

Mr. Kim assigned them a project that Friday: build a poster explaining how natural selection shaped the beaks of finches on the Galápagos Islands. Aurora got the library book. Kurtis got a bag of sunflower seeds, two spoons, and a pair of tweezers, because Kurtis believed every problem could be solved with snacks.

They set up on the lunch table outside. Kurtis pinched the tweezers like a beak and tried to pick up a seed. It shot across the table and hit him in the chin. His reflex was to blame the tweezers, so he threw them on the ground and crossed his arms, obstinate as a mule.

"Try the spoon," Aurora said. "A big beak cracks seeds. A skinny beak picks bugs out of bark." She held up the library book, which had a picture of three finches side by side, beaks like different tools in the same drawer. "The ones on islands with hard seeds got big beaks, because the birds that could crack them didn't starve."

"So the beaks are different because the food is different," Kurtis said. He tried the spoon. The seed cracked. He ate it anyway, which was against the rules of the experiment, and Jaydon wrote "data contamination" on the poster.

Aurora flipped a page and stopped. "Listen to this. Darwin collected those birds and thought they were wrens and blackbirds."

Jaydon laughed so hard he knocked over the seed bag. "Darwin? The Darwin?"

"In 1837," Aurora read on, "a bird scientist named John Gould looked at them and told Darwin they were actually a whole new group of closely related finches." She looked up. "Darwin misidentified a bird."

Jaydon was quiet for a second. "So a genius got it wrong too."

"He got it wrong, and then he figured it out," Aurora said. She wrote 1837, John Gould, finches in the corner of the poster. "That's the good part."

On Monday they presented the poster. At the end, Mr. Kim asked if there were questions, and Aurora raised her own hand. "One. The bird at the feeder was a female red-winged blackbird. I looked it up."

Jaydon whispered, "So you were right."

"Half right," Aurora said, and taped the spoon to the poster.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals.
story:
Claire spread her Charter of Rights and Freedoms booklet across the table in the community centre craft room and read the same section for the third time. Her assignment was to pick one right and explain it in her own words at Thursday's meeting of the after-school civics club, and she had chosen section 15, equal treatment under the law, mostly because it sounded important. The problem was that every time she tried to write her explanation, Arianna's voice kept interrupting her in her head.

Arianna had been angry all week. On Saturday the two of them had gone to the corner store near the community centre to buy synthetic turf scraps for the club's mini putting green project, and the cashier had pointed at a new sign that said NO BACKPACKS and made them leave their bags behind the counter. Arianna had refused, and they had ended up buying nothing. "They can't do that," Arianna had said on the walk home. "The Charter says equal treatment. The store is breaking it." Claire hadn't known what to say then, but now, with the booklet open in front of her, she noticed something she had missed in class. The words on the page kept saying "government" this and "law" that, and nowhere did they say anything about stores.

She tested her idea the way Mr. Lewandowski, the club leader, had shown them with the robotics kit last month: change one thing and see what happens. She covered the word "government" with her thumb and read the sentence aloud. It fell apart. Every right in her section applied to laws, to governments, to things done under government authority. She uncovered her thumb and read it again, and the whole page rearranged itself in her mind. "It's like the motion sensor we installed on the door," she said to herself. "It only sees what moves in front of it. The Charter only reaches what governments do." A private store banning backpacks was a different kind of rule, the kind the province's laws about businesses would handle, not the Charter.

At Thursday's meeting, Claire stood up with her page of notes. She explained section 15 in her own words, then added, "And here's the part I got wrong all week. I thought a store near us broke the Charter by banning backpacks. It didn't, because the Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals." Arianna's hand shot up. "So the store can just do that?" "Not forever," Claire said. "Franco's cousin complained to a provincial office and got a letter back. There's a rule, it's just not this rule."

After the meeting, Arianna dumped her backpack on the craft table and pulled out two sheets of leftover turf. "For the putting green. I went back today, no backpack, carried it." She smoothed the synthetic grass flat with her palm.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Many camps use a buddy system at the waterfront: each swimmer is paired with a partner, and at a 'buddy check' the pairs must find each other quickly so staff can count everyone.
story:
The campfire snapped and threw sparks into the dark, and Daniel turned his marshmallow on a stick without really watching it. Beside him, Yassine kept glancing across the circle at a girl named on nobody's lips yet, a girl who had come back from swim time late and dripping and quiet.

"She was with me," William whispered, leaning over. "In the water, I mean. Then she wasn't."

Daniel thought about that. At the lake, a whistle had blown, and everyone had scrambled to find their partner and hold up linked hands while the lifeguards counted. He remembered William standing alone in the shallows, scanning the water with a face gone pale. At the time Daniel had thought William was afraid of the fish, or of the cold. Now he wasn't so sure.

"Why did you look so scared when the whistle went?" Daniel asked him. "You were standing in two feet of water."

"It's called a buddy check," William said. "You have to find your buddy fast, so the staff can count everybody." He poked at the fire with a long branch, and an ember rolled. "If your buddy isn't there, they think something happened to her. In the water. Under it."

Yassine went very still. "She just walked off to the canteen," he said. "I saw her go. I didn't think it mattered."

It was a small thing, Daniel thought, the kind of choice that seemed small right up until it wasn't. The whistle, the counting, the linked hands. A rule with a shape you couldn't see, but you could see what it did to William's face. He tested it out loud, slowly. "So when the whistle blows, whoever you're paired with has to show up. If she'd drowned, that would be the only way to know. That's why he looked like that."

Yassine nodded, staring into the flames like they might console him. They didn't.

When the marshmallows were gone and the fire had burned down to a corrosive orange shell of ash around the coals, Yassine stood up. He crossed the circle, crouched next to the girl, and said something too low for Daniel to hear. She looked up, then at William, then down at her hands. Slowly she got up and walked around the fire to stand in front of him.

"I didn't know," she said. "I thought the whistle was for lunch."

William laughed, a shaky laugh, and stuck out his hand. "Tomorrow, when it blows, you find me. Deal?"

"Deal," she said, and shook it.

Mr. Wanjiru, who had been quiet all evening by the log pile, leaned toward the flames and said, "First nights are always like this. By Thursday you'll all be telling this story like it was funny." He nudged a fresh log into the fire, and the sparks climbed again, higher than before.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
Aiden stood in Grandma's kitchen holding a heavy pot and a bag of sugar, because tonight he was making dessert for the whole family and he had exactly one plan: caramel. Jad and Asha had come along for the weekend, and they were already arguing about who got to lick the spoon.

"It's a privilege," Aiden told them, setting the pot on the stove. "I am the chef. You are the helpers."

Jad leaned over the pot, sniffing. "How do you even know it'll turn brown? Right now it's just white sugar."

"I hypothesize that heat does it," Aiden said. "Sugar alone, plus heat, equals brown. That's my whole hypothesis."

While the sugar melted, the roast in the oven filled the kitchen with a smell that made Asha groan out loud. "Okay but here's my question," she said, poking at the oven door. "Is the caramel the same browning as the crust on that roast? They're both brown. Both from heat."

Jad shrugged. "Obviously the same thing. Browning is browning."

Aiden stirred the sugar and thought hard. Something didn't fit. "Wait. The crust is on meat. Meat isn't just sugar. It's got protein in it, and protein has amino acids." He said the word slowly, remembering it from a cereal box he'd read once, of all things. "My caramel is sugar and nothing else. So if my browning only needs sugar, and the roast's browning needs amino acids too, they can't be the same reaction."

"So test it," Asha said. "You're always saying test it."

He did. He took two small spoonfuls of plain sugar and heated one with a pinch of baking soda, since the box claimed amino acids were in basically everything, and left the other alone. Both browned, but the plain sugar browned faster and smelled different, like candy instead of dinner. He wrote the results on a napkin with a greasy pencil: sugar alone, browning. Sugar with extra amino acids, different browning, slower, smells like roast.

"Caramelization," he announced, holding up the napkin like a trophy. "Sugar alone, heated, and it browns. It's called caramelization."

"Then what's the roast one called?" Jad asked.

Aiden frowned. The napkin didn't say. Then, from the doorway, Ms. Eze, the neighbour who always showed up when something smelled good, pointed at the oven. "The Maillard reaction," she said, and stole a strawberry from the bowl. "Needs the amino acids. Not my area, but my husband won't stop talking about it."

"Ha!" Asha pointed at Jad. "You owe me a dollar. Browning is not browning."

The caramel, meanwhile, had gone from golden to a shade Aiden could only describe as aggressive. He yanked it off the heat, poured it over the strawberries, and held his breath. It hardened with a crackle, glossy and amber, and when they cracked it with spoons it shattered like thin ice.

Grandma got the first piece. She bit down, listened to the crunch, and nodded once. "Second pot tomorrow," she said. "You're the chef now. Those two are still just helpers."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
The poster project was due Friday, and Thomas's group had nothing but a blank sheet of paper. Ms. Charles had assigned each group a decade and a stack of old magazines, asking them to find examples of persuasion in wartime ads. Thomas spread the magazines across the desk while Azaan volunteered to coordinate who cut, who glued, and who wrote the labels.

"Look at this one," Rayane said, holding up a soda ad with a famous baseball player grinning over a bottle. "If he drinks it, everyone will think it's great." Thomas wrote "celebrity testimonial" on a sticky note. The next ad showed a crowd of smiling faces with the words "Everybody's switching," and Azaan slapped it down beside a war poster that shouted "Millions have joined!" Bandwagon, they labeled it, and after that they spotted loaded words everywhere, "freedom," "pure," "the enemy's lies," words designed to stir feelings.

But when Rayane found a cereal box ad saying "all-natural goodness," the group stalled. "What kind of technique is that?" she asked. "It's not a celebrity. It's not a crowd." Thomas flipped the box over and read the ingredient list out loud. "Corn syrup, red dye, flavoring. There's a synthetic vitamin in here. It doesn't say anything you can actually check." He stared at the word "goodness" on the front, then at "natural," and something clicked. "They're vague. Positive. They just make you feel good."

"Glittering generalities," said Ms. Charles from the next row, passing by with a stack of papers. "That's what they're called." Thomas wrote the words on a label, but he didn't stop there. He had an idea, and he wanted to test it. "Let's count how many ads in the whole stack use words nobody can prove. If glittering generalities are everywhere, we can make that the headline of our poster."

For twenty minutes the three of them worked like a courtroom, with each ad put on trial. Rayane acted as the defendant, arguing that "pure" might mean something, while Thomas cross-examined: "Pure what? Measured how?" If she couldn't answer, the ad went in the guilty pile. Azaan kept tally. By the end they had fourteen ads in the pile, more than bandwagon and celebrity combined, and Thomas felt the kind of satisfaction that only comes from counting something yourself.

On Friday they presented the poster, glittery title and all, and Ms. Charles asked the class which technique was hardest to spot. Rayane pointed at the cereal box. "This one," she said. "Because it sounds so nice." Thomas held up the box with the ingredient list facing out and tapped the word "natural." "Nice isn't the same as true," he said. "Flip it over and see."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When the price of one good rises, many buyers switch to a substitute, a similar good that does the same job, so demand for the substitute goes up.
story:
The jar on Mr. Wang's shelf held exactly six monarch larva, and every kid in seventh period wanted to take one home for the weekend. Mr. Wang said only one rule would govern it: whoever wanted one had to trade in two homework passes. Nobody had homework passes to spare except Quinn, who saved everything, and Quinn was home sick.

Charles wanted a larva more than he had wanted anything since the winter his grandmother knitted him a scarf with his initials. He had exactly one homework pass. He stood at the shelf while David counted his own passes and got to one and stopped. "This is a disaster," David said. "It's a bug." "It's a monarch," Charles said, as if that settled it.

Then Quinn walked in, pale but upright, holding two passes. Charles watched him hand them over and take the largest larva, the one already thick and quiet on its milkweed. Charles noticed something else too. Two kids who had been hovering at the shelf drifted over to the aquarium by the window, where Mrs. Olvera's class kept tadpoles, and started asking if they could take one of those home instead. A tadpole was not a monarch larva, but it was still a thing that turned into something else, and it cost nothing. By lunch, the tadpole tank was nearly empty and nobody was standing at Mr. Wang's shelf anymore.

That afternoon at the student store, where Charles worked the Tuesday shift, he tested what he had seen. The chocolate chip cookies came in only two boxes that day, so the manager had raised them from fifty cents to a dollar. Charles watched kid after kid look at the sign, wince, and buy the oatmeal ones at the old price. The oatmeal ones did the same job, in the way that a cookie does a job. "They're switching," Charles told David, who had come by for a snack. "The cookies got expensive, so everyone moves to the next-best thing. Mr. Wang calls those substitutes." "You're explaining my own snack to me," David said, taking his oatmeal cookie and the last bag of the oatmeal ones off the shelf behind it.

Charles marked the oatmeal shortage in the inventory book, then flipped the sign on the chocolate chip cookies back to fifty cents. They sold out in four minutes anyway, since there were only six left, and he wrote "temporary" next to the whole mess in the margin. On his way out he passed the window aquarium, empty now except for one tadpole nobody had wanted, swimming slow circles like it knew.
